newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - Greyhound targets US-Mexico travel.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Greyhound targets US-Mexico travel.

text.p: Greyhound Lines Inc is hoping a strategy to expand U.S.-Mexico passenger service will bring $50 to $100 million in annual revenues, starting in three or four years, chief executive Craig Lentzsch said Friday.
The goal is to let passengers between travel between U.S. and Mexican cities without switching buses at the border.

Lentzsch said Greyhound has invested $3 million to $4 million so far on the plan, excluding the recent cash-and stock purchase of Valley Transit, a company serving South Texas with $10 million a year in revenues and 74 buses.
Earnings accretion from the purchase of Valley Transit could begin in the third or fourth quarter, depending on when the Surface Transportation Board approves the deal, Lentzsch said.
The purchase gives Greyhound access to Valley Transit buses that are licensed to operate in Mexico.

"It gives us a business that is very effective in the Spanish language market on the U.S. side of the border, and it makes it very easy for us to create cross-border service," Lentzsch told Reuters. "They already own buses that are legal to operate in Mexico, and we don't."

Greyhound hopes to strengthen cross-border passenger sales, Lentzsch said, reversing a trend in which it has been losing market share along the border to small competitors such as van operators and Spanish-language bus operators.
Greyhound will invest $25 to $30 million on the plan, which could include acquisitions of more U.S. bus companies or investments in Mexican companies, said Lentzsch, who is also company president.
"It's a practical thing to do. It's a growing market and it's a bus-oriented market," Lentzsch said.
"We think the border market is growing about 20 percent per year, and the rest of our business is growing about five or six percent per year," he added. "That's what the market research tells us."
Dallas-based Greyhound, which has about $700.8 million in yearly revenues, is the oldest U.S. intercity bus service and the only one still operating nationwide.
It has been negotiating with Mexican carriers for a year and a half to create coordinated, cooperative cross-border service, Lentzsch said.

In January the company started service from Los Angeles to Cuidad Obregon, 600 miles into Mexico. That service relies on a joint operating agreement with Crucero SA, a Mexican partner that is licensed to run its buses in the United States.
